title: Field Report: Filling the Boxes at Night

post.author: u/night_manager_pasquale
post.title: I manage a gaming café at night. Our game cache fills itself the way a Netflix post from 2016 says. Last night, mid-tournament, a game nobody was playing took 98% of our line.

blocks.text: I'm Pasquale, night manager at Duskcade Thornaby, one of the Duskcade chain's 20 gaming cafés: 40 seats, each a gaming computer. We're busiest from midnight to 04:00. Our quiet hours, when the fewest seats are taken, are 08:00 to 12:00.
Games are huge, so every café keeps a cache server: a back-room computer holding copies of the games our seats play. A cache is a saved copy kept close. Seats install from it in minutes.
Everything else comes down our line, the café's one connection to the internet: 100 Mbps, megabits a second. An online match sends only small messages, but it hates waiting.
The tournament screen shows each player's ping: how long a message takes to reach the game's server and back, in ms (thousandths of a second). Ours is usually 20.
The caches are filled by the chain's central system, at head office in Yelverton, on a line big enough to feed all 20 at once.

Fiametta built it in 2025 from a printout: "Netflix and Fill", Netflix TechBlog, 11 August 2016. Netflix fills its boxes, Open Connect appliances inside internet companies' networks, "proactively during configured fill windows": set hours when a box may download.

Ours fills in four steps. The central system predicts which games each café will want and sends each cache its list. In the fill window, each cache asks for whatever on its list it lacks, then downloads it at full line speed.

Fiametta set one window for all 20 cafés: 02:00 to 06:00. The post gives no hours; those are when a streaming service's viewers sleep. The fill has a speed cap, the most of the line a fill may take. Ours says "full line".

Most nights the fill is patches, small updates of 2 to 5 GB (gigabytes): 2 min 40 s to 6 min 40 s at full line. Some nights a player swore at a spike just after two. It passed; we blamed the game's servers.

Last night, Thursday 15 October, was our league final: 40 players, every seat, from midnight. At 00:00 the central system listed Gravewake, a 60 GB game unlocking at 00:00 Saturday. 60 GB × 8 ÷ 100 Mbps = 4,800 seconds: 80 minutes of a full line.

At 02:01 the room started shouting "lag". Every ping read 900. I opened the line graph our router draws (the router: the box joining us to the line): one point a minute, the share of the line in use. My notes: time, line used, worst ping, cache:

01:50  line  0%  ping  20 ms  idle, Gravewake listed
02:01  line 98%  ping 900 ms  filling since 02:00
02:30  line 98%  ping 900 ms  22.5 of 60 GB
03:21  line  0%  ping  20 ms  done 03:20, 60 of 60 GB

Nobody was downloading; all 40 seats played installed games. Why 98%, not 100%? Our provider runs the line 2% above the 100 Mbps we pay for, to carry the small label on every piece of data. The graph counts against that: full reads 98%.

blocks.label: line_graph_fri_0130_0400.png

diagram.aria: Friday 16 October 2026, 01:30 to 04:00. The 40 matches run at a 20 ms ping until 02:00, at 900 ms from 02:00 to 03:20, and at 20 ms again after. The Gravewake fill, 60 GB, waits listed until the window opens at 02:00 and runs at full line from 02:00 to 03:20. For comparison, a usual night's 5 GB patch runs from 02:00 to 02:06:40. A marker at 02:30 shows the line at 98%.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the router's line graph and my notes, Friday 16 October 2026. Red: from 02:00 to 03:20 the fill took the full line and every ping in the league final read 900 ms instead of 20. Amber, for comparison: a usual night's 5 GB patch, over by 02:06:40, the spike nobody traced.

blocks.text: The cache did exactly what it was told, at exactly the hour it was told.
We paused the final at 02:05 and restarted after 03:20 with whoever stayed. The next big release will be listed the same way. What should Duskcade change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Two words, then questions. When data arrives faster than a line can carry it, your router keeps the extra in a waiting room, a queue, and sends it out in order. Anything that arrives behind a full queue waits its turn, a match message included. Bandwidth, how much a line carries each second, is not delay, how long one message takes (The Voice on Line Two). Now your notes. At 02:01, how much of the line did your 40 matches need, and how much did the fill take? Whose quiet hours are 02:00 to 06:00, and whose are yours? And on patch nights, how long did the spike after two last?

replies.author: u/night_manager_pasquale
replies.text: Fiametta checked. The central system has one window setting, "all sites 02:00 to 06:00", and one speed cap, "full line". All 20 cafés' graphs show the same block, 02:00 to 03:20. On patch nights ours spikes for a few minutes after two, every night since the system went live.

comments.author: u/just_buy_fibre_amalric
comments.text: Bandwidth is cheap; a faster line ends the problem. Get fibre, a line of glass threads that carries far more: 500 Mbps for each café costs a bit more a month than you pay now. At 500 the same 60 GB takes 960 seconds, 16 minutes, and a patch is gone in 80 seconds. Nobody rebuilds a clever system for a problem money fixes by Friday.

comments.author: u/whole_list_teofil
comments.text: The weak spot is the guessing. Fiametta's system predicts which games each café wants; guess wrong and a player waits on the internet. Skip the predictions. Fill the chain's whole game list, every game it carries, into every café, with every update, every night. That's about 15 GB a night more than your list. Disks are cheap, and nothing is ever missing.

comments.author: u/pull_through_dagmar
comments.text: Why fill ahead at all? Most CDNs, networks of caches kept near users (see Mirrors Everywhere), fetch on first request, in steps. A player asks the cache for a game. If the cache hasn't got it, it fetches it from the central system, keeps a copy and hands it over. Every later player gets the copy. That's a pull-through cache. No predictions, no window, and nothing downloads that nobody asked for.

reply.prompt: The next big release will be listed the same way, and every cache will fetch it in the same window. What should Duskcade change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Buy each café a faster line, so the night's fill is done before anyone notices it.
options.verdict: A bigger line, filled just as full
options.part2: By November all 20 cafés had fibre: 500 Mbps, with new routers whose waiting room holds the same 880 ms of the line. Patch nights went quiet: a 5 GB patch took 1 min 20 s. On Friday 13 November the central system listed Gravewake's 60 GB expansion at midnight, to unlock on Saturday, and at 02:00 the cache took the new line exactly as it had taken the old one: 98% on the graph and every ping on our league night at 900 ms until 02:16. We paused the matches again. The installed games were fine and the expansion was on the cache by morning; the league night lost 16 minutes, and the chain's bill went up every month. In the sim, set the line to 500 Mbps: the fill runs 02:00 to 02:16, 16 minutes, all of it at 900 ms in peak.
options.senior: The fill's speed cap said "full line", so it takes whatever line you buy. A faster line shortens the harm; it doesn't remove it, because ping depends on the waiting room being full, not on the line's size. Filling faster to finish sooner is the same mistake: bandwidth and delay are different things. Spend on bandwidth when the busy-hour traffic itself has outgrown the line; for a transfer you control, change when it runs and how much of the line it may take.

options.text: Fill the whole game list into every café every night, so nothing is ever missing.
options.verdict: Bigger fills at the same bad hour
options.part2: From November every cache took every update for every game on the chain's list: about 15 GB a night more. A usual patch night went from 5 GB to 20 GB: 26 min 40 s of full line after two, every night, in the busiest hours. On Friday 13 November Gravewake's 60 GB expansion came with 15 GB of updates for games nobody in Thornaby plays: 75 GB, 02:00 to 03:40, and our league night spent 100 minutes at 900 ms. The installed games were all up to date and the expansion was ready for Saturday; nobody could play the matches. In the sim, turn on fill everything: 100 minutes at 900 ms in peak tonight, and a patch night's 20 GB takes 26 min 40 s.
options.senior: Filling everything trades a prediction problem for a size problem, and the size lands in the same window. Predictions exist so each place holds what it will use; Netflix's post describes popularity rankings computed by country and region for exactly that. A wrong guess costs one player a wait; filling everything costs every player the line, every night, and fills every cache's disks with games its café never plays.

options.text: Fill each café in its own quiet hours, and cap the fill to a share of the line.
options.part2: Fiametta made the fill window a setting per café, taken from each café's own graph of seats in use, and added a cap. Thornaby's window is now 08:00 to 12:00, capped at 40 Mbps, and each of the other 19 got its own hours. On Friday 13 November Gravewake's 60 GB expansion was listed at midnight. Our league night ran clean: ping 20 all night. At 08:00 the fill began; the graph sat at 39% all morning, the few early players kept their 20 ms, and at 11:20 the 60 GB was on the cache: 12,000 seconds, 3 h 20 min. At midnight on Saturday the first player installed it from the back room in minutes. In the sim, choose 08:00 to 12:00 and 40 Mbps: the fill runs 08:00 to 11:20, the line reads 39%, and no minute of peak reaches 900 ms.
options.senior: Keep the predictions and the push; fix the hour and the share. A fill window should come from each place's own measured quiet hours, not from someone else's sleep, and a fill should be capped so whoever is there still gets the line. Then check that the biggest fill fits: a 4-hour window at 40 Mbps holds 72 GB, so a bigger release must be listed earlier and filled over more than one window. Netflix's post describes the same shape: windows configured per place, using non-peak bandwidth, with the fill moving across time zones.

options.text: Stop filling ahead; fetch each file the first time a player in that café asks for it.
options.verdict: Trade-off: no night fill, a peak fetch instead
options.part2: Fiametta switched the fill off; each cache now fetches a game the first time a seat asks. Friday 13 November's league night ran clean: nothing downloaded at 02:00. At 00:00 on Saturday the expansion unlocked and the first player in Thornaby asked for it at once. The cache hadn't got it, so it fetched all 60 GB at full line, 00:00 to 01:20. That player waited 80 minutes, and every match in a full Saturday room read 900 for the same 80 minutes. All 20 caches pulled it from Yelverton in the same minute. The installed games were fine; the expansion arrived at peak, through the busiest hour. In the sim, choose fetch on first request: Friday stays quiet, the first player waits 80 minutes, and Saturday has 80 minutes at 900 ms in peak.
options.senior: Pull-through is the right default when you can't predict what will be asked for, or when files are small and requests spread out: the first asker pays a short wait and nothing unwanted moves. It is the wrong tool for a big, predictable launch, because the first request comes at the moment of most demand, so the download lands in the peak it was meant to avoid. Many systems mix the two: push what you can predict in quiet hours, pull the long tail on demand.

sim.title: Replay Duskcade Thornaby's line, Friday and Saturday
sim.lede: You're Pasquale, replaying two days at Duskcade Thornaby from Friday 16 October 2026, 00:00, in 10-minute steps. As given data: the line carries 100 Mbps of data, and the provider runs it 2% above that for the label on each piece, so the graph reads a full line as 98%. 1 GB is 8,000 megabits, so 60 GB at 100 Mbps takes 4,800 seconds. The central system lists the file at Friday 00:00. Fill ahead downloads it in the fill window each day, at the rate the speed cap allows, the release first; whatever is left when the window ends waits for the next day's window. Fetch on first request fills nothing ahead: the first player to want the file asks at 00:00 on Saturday, when it unlocks, and the cache fetches it then. Peak is 00:00 to 04:00; Thornaby's quiet hours are 08:00 to 12:00. Ping is 20 ms at rest. While a fill takes the full line, the router's waiting room stays full and holds 880 ms of the line, so every ping is 900 ms (the 500 Mbps line's router is set the same way); a capped fill leaves room, and ping stays 20 ms. The matches' own traffic is too small to change any sum here. Fill everything adds every other game's updates: 15 GB tonight.
sim.tryThis: Try this: step to Friday 02:30 as built: the line reads 98%, ping 900 ms, 22.5 of 60 GB, and the fill is done at 03:20 after 80 minutes, all of it in peak. Switch to a 5 GB patch: 6 min 40 s. Now choose 08:00 to 12:00 and 40 Mbps: 08:00 to 11:20, the line at 39%, ping 20 ms. Try a 500 Mbps line (16 minutes at 900 ms), fill everything (100 minutes), and fetch on first request (the first player waits 80 minutes on Saturday). Last, a 90 GB release with the fix.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke. Duskcade copied Netflix's fill, predicting, listing and downloading ahead in a window, but set one window for all 20 cafés from a streaming service's sleeping hours, which are a gaming café's busiest, and let the fill take the full line. The first fill big enough to last, 60 GB, held the line at 98% for 80 minutes in the middle of a league final.

steps.title: Two ways to fill a cache: pull when asked, or push ahead.
steps.text: A pull-through cache, the way most commercial CDNs work (Mirrors Everywhere), runs in steps. First a player asks for a file. The cache looks for its copy; the first time, it has none, a miss. It fetches the file from the origin, keeps a copy and hands it over. Every later request is a hit. What can go wrong: the first asker waits for the whole fetch, at whatever hour they ask. Open Connect pushes instead, in four steps. First, predict what members will watch and when. Second, give each appliance a manifest, the list of what it should hold. Third, during its configured fill window, each appliance asks for what it lacks and is given a ranked list of places to download from. Fourth, serve members from the copy, with no first-request wait. What can go wrong: a wrong prediction leaves a gap, and a window set at the wrong hour fills during the busy time. Duskcade copied all four steps; the third ran at the wrong hour.

steps.title: A full line means a full waiting room, and a 900 ms ping.
steps.text: When data arrives faster than a line can send it, the router queues the rest in a waiting room and sends it in order. A fill at full line speed keeps that room full: Thornaby's router holds 880 ms of the line, so every match message waited 880 ms behind game data, and the ping went from 20 to 900. Bandwidth is how much fits through; delay is how long one message waits (The Voice on Line Two). The 40 matches needed almost none of the line, and all of its speed. A 5 GB patch held the room full for 6 min 40 s, a spike nobody traced; 60 GB held it for 80 minutes. Filling faster to finish sooner does not help: a 500 Mbps line ends the fill in 16 minutes, and those 16 minutes still read 900, because the fill takes the whole of whatever line it has.

steps.title: The window belongs to the place, not to the copy.
steps.text: Netflix's post says it can use non-peak bandwidth because it predicts what members will watch and what time of day they will watch it, and that each appliance asks during its configured fill window. It also describes the window ending in one time zone as members start watching, and the fill carrying on as the window moves to other time zones: each place fills in its own quiet hours. Duskcade copied the window but not the per-place part: one setting, 02:00 to 06:00, chosen from a streaming service's sleep, for 20 cafés whose busiest hours are midnight to 04:00. The right window comes from each café's own graph of seats in use. Thornaby's quietest hours are 08:00 to 12:00.

steps.title: A cap keeps a share of the line for whoever is there.
steps.text: Even in quiet hours somebody plays. A cap limits the fill to a share of the line. At 40 Mbps, 60 GB × 8 ÷ 40 = 12,000 seconds, 3 h 20 min, from 08:00 to 11:20, with the graph at 39% and the waiting room empty, so pings stay at 20. The cost is time: a 4-hour window at 40 Mbps holds 72 GB at most, so check every listing against that before its window. Filling everything every night makes each fill bigger at the same hour: 75 GB took 100 minutes at full line, and even with the fix it spills 3 GB into Saturday morning.

steps.title: The walk to Yelverton.
steps.text: Everything in Pasquale's café worked: the cache, the router, the seats, the graph. The cause sat in a building Pasquale had never seen. On Monday they took the train to Yelverton with Fiametta. The chain's data room was cold and loud. On the wall screen were 20 small line graphs, one per café, each with the same block at 02:00, the same height, the same width, like 20 prints of one photograph. Taped to the rack below was the printout, "configured fill windows" circled in pen, and beside it the one line Fiametta had typed in 2025: all sites, 02:00 to 06:00, full line.

diagram.aria: The fix. The central system in Yelverton still predicts and lists. It sends Thornaby's cache its list and its own window, 08:00 to 12:00, with the fill capped at 40 Mbps. The cache serves the 40 seats, whose ping stays 20 ms through the peak, midnight to 04:00. Below: the window comes from each café's own quiet hours, and every listing is checked against what a window can hold, 72 GB at 40 Mbps.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next release. The central system keeps predicting and listing, but each café's window now comes from that café's own quiet hours, Thornaby's 08:00 to 12:00, and the fill is capped at 40 Mbps. Every listing is checked against what one window can hold. In the sim: 60 GB from 08:00 to 11:20, the line at 39%, ping 20 ms all day.

fix.title: The fix: each café's own window, a capped fill, and a check that it fits
fix.text: Keep the predictions and the push; they are why a 60 GB game can be ready the moment it unlocks. Make the fill window a per-café setting, taken from each café's own measured quiet hours, and review it when the café's hours change. Cap the fill to a share of the line, 40 Mbps of Thornaby's 100, so whoever is playing in the morning keeps a 20 ms ping. Before each night, check every listing against what the café's window can hold at that cap, 72 GB for 4 hours at 40 Mbps; list anything bigger earlier, so it fills over several windows, and raise an alert for any cache that will not hold its list in time.

limits: Quiet hours are measured, and they move: a café near a university, a holiday week, a new tournament night. A window chosen once goes stale; review each café's graph every few months.
A cap makes fills slower. 40 Mbps for 4 hours holds 72 GB, so a bigger release must be listed days earlier or it is not ready at the unlock.
Predictions still miss. A game nobody predicted for Thornaby has to come over the line when someone asks, at whatever hour; the cap and the window do nothing for it.

No minute of peak at 900 ms.

explain.seniorTake: Copying a system means copying its reasons, not only its shape. Netflix fills ahead because it can predict what each place will watch and when, and it fills in windows set per place, in each place's own non-peak hours. Duskcade copied the push and the window and left out the per-place part, so a streaming service's quiet hours became a gaming café's busiest. Any big background transfer, a fill, a backup, a copy between regions, needs three answers: when is this place quiet, how much of the line may it take, and will it finish before it is needed. Staff work is walking into the building where the one setting for all sites was typed, and asking whose hours it came from.

realWorld.title: Netflix and Fill, 2016: proactive caching
realWorld.text: Costello and Livengood write: "An important difference between our Open Connect CDN and other commercial CDNs is the concept of proactive caching." And: "We deploy the majority of our updates proactively during configured fill windows". A commercial pull-through CDN waits for a request; Open Connect fills ahead.

realWorld.title: Predicting the hour, not only the title
realWorld.text: "Because we can predict with high accuracy what our members will watch and what time of day they will watch it, we can make use of non-peak bandwidth to download most of the content updates to the OCAs in our network during these configurable time windows."

realWorld.title: A finite window every day
realWorld.text: "The predictability of off-peak traffic patterns helps with this optimization, but we still only have a finite amount of time every day to get our content pre-positioned to where it needs to be before our traffic starts to ramp up and we want to make all of the OCA capacity available for content serving."

realWorld.title: Each appliance asks in its own window
realWorld.text: "If there is a delta between the list of titles in the manifest and what they are currently storing, each OCA will send a request, during its configured fill window, that includes a list of the new or updated titles that it needs." The post also describes the window ending in one time zone as members begin streaming and the fill continuing as the window moves to other time zones.

realWorld.title: Watching the fill
realWorld.text: "The Open Connect Operations team uses internal tooling to constantly monitor our fill traffic, and alerts are set and monitored for OCAs that do not contain a threshold percentage of the catalog that they are supposed to be serving to members." The post also describes out-of-cycle fast track fills for new titles or urgent fixes, following the same fill patterns more quickly.

realWorld.title: Open Connect: boxes inside internet companies' networks
realWorld.text: Netflix's Open Connect site says: "Open Connect Appliances can be embedded in your ISP network." And: "Embedded OCAs have the same capabilities as the OCAs that we use in our 60+ global data centers, and they are provided to qualifying ISP partners at no charge."

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8.6: capacity management
realWorld.text: ISMS.online's summary of the control says: "The control emphasises monitoring, stress testing, and planning for scalability to maintain business continuity." A summary page, not the standard's own text, which is paid.

asked: Push or pull CDN: when do you fill ahead?
How do you schedule big background transfers without hurting live traffic?
interview.answer: I'd put caching boxes as close to viewers as possible, inside internet companies' networks where they'll host them, so most video never crosses the wider internet. Then I'd decide push or pull per kind of content. Popular, predictable titles I'd push: predict what each region will watch, give each box a list of what to hold, and fill it ahead during that region's own off-peak window, so viewers never wait for a first-request miss. The long tail I'd pull through on demand, because predicting it costs more than the occasional wait. For any big background transfer I ask three questions. When is this place quiet, measured from its own traffic rather than head office's clock? How much of the link may the transfer take, so live traffic keeps its share and its delay stays low? And will it finish before it's needed, given that window and that cap? If not, start it earlier over several windows, and alert on any box that won't hold its list in time. I'd tell the story of a gaming-café chain that copied one fill window from a streaming service's sleeping hours to all its sites, and filled a 60 GB game into the middle of a tournament.

atWork: One schedule copied to every site is a common pattern: a backup, a software update, a copy between regions or a cache fill set once at head office's quiet hour and applied everywhere, whatever each site's own busy hours are. Find your big background transfers and check four things. Where did each one's window come from: the site's own measured traffic, or someone's clock? How much of the link may it take, and is there a cap at all? What is the biggest transfer it has ever run, and would the next one finish inside the window at that cap? And who is alerted when a transfer runs into busy hours or won't finish before it's needed? On AWS, the same questions apply to Systems Manager maintenance windows, AWS Backup plans and cross-region replication: are they set per region, in that region's own quiet hours? Standards, stated conditionally: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.6 (capacity management) is where an auditor would look for monitored link use and planned capacity, and a per-site window with a cap and a record of each transfer's size and duration is the kind of evidence it asks for, so build it in from the first design, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company has 30 shops in several countries. Each shop's server downloads the nightly price file and software updates at 01:00 head-office time, at full speed. Shops on the far side of the world say their tills slow down every evening around 18:00 their time. What is happening, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: One head-office hour lands in some shops' busy hours; set each shop's window from its own quiet hours
Limit the download to a share of the shop's link so live traffic keeps room
Measure each shop's busy and quiet hours from its own traffic, and check the transfer fits

recall.model: The download runs at full speed at 01:00 head-office time, which on the far side of the world is 18:00, the shops' busy evening, so it fills each shop's link while the tills are trading and every till message waits behind it. I'd give every shop its own window, taken from its own quiet hours, which I'd measure from each shop's own traffic graph rather than guess. I'd also cap the download to a share of the link, so even a shop that is busy during its window keeps room for the tills. Then I'd check that the biggest file fits in each shop's window at that cap, and start bigger ones a night earlier.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with the 60 GB release, which settings keep every ping at 20 ms on both days and still have the release on the cache before the Saturday 00:00 unlock?
options: A 500 Mbps line, everything else as built
The 08:00 to 12:00 window at full line
The 08:00 to 12:00 window, capped at 40 Mbps
recall.why: Capped at 40 Mbps from 08:00, the fill runs 08:00 to 11:20 with the line at 39% and ping 20 ms throughout, and the release is on the cache long before the unlock. A 500 Mbps line still spends 16 minutes at 900 ms in peak; the 08:00 window at full line spends 80 minutes at 900 ms in the morning; fetch on first request spends 80 minutes at 900 ms in Saturday's peak while the first player waits.

recall.prompt: According to "Netflix and Fill", when does each Open Connect appliance send its request for the new or updated titles it needs?
options: The moment a member presses Play
At one fixed hour for the whole network
recall.why: The post says: "each OCA will send a request, during its configured fill window, that includes a list of the new or updated titles that it needs." It describes the window ending in one time zone and moving on to others, not one hour for the whole network, and pressing Play is when a commercial pull-through CDN would first fetch.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: push or pull CDN, when do you fill ahead, and how do you keep a big fill from hurting live traffic?

keyIdeas.idea: Push what you can predict, such as popular titles and launches
Pull the long tail on demand, accepting a first-request wait
Fill in each place's own off-peak window
Cap the fill to a share of the link and check it finishes in time

recall.model: Push what I can predict: popular titles and big launches go into each cache ahead of time, so nobody waits on a first request. Pull the long tail on demand through the cache, because predicting it costs more than the occasional wait. Every fill runs in that place's own off-peak window, measured from its own traffic, not head office's clock, and it's capped to a share of the link so live traffic keeps its room and its delay stays low. Then I check that the biggest fill finishes inside the window at that cap, start bigger ones earlier, and alert on any cache that won't hold its list in time.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The windows work: Thornaby fills from 08:00 to 12:00 at 40 Mbps, and no league night has lagged since October. On Friday 15 January 2027 at 00:00 the central system listed Gravewake's second expansion, 90 GB, to unlock at 00:00 on Saturday 16 January. At midnight the room asked for it. The cache held 72 GB of the 90. A seat can't install part of a game, and the cache would fetch the last 18 GB only in Saturday's window, so the first players waited until 09:00: 9 hours. Under the old 02:00 window at full line, it would have been ready by 04:00 on Friday, with two hours of 900 ms ping on the league night.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why wasn't the expansion ready at midnight, and what should change so it doesn't happen again?

keyIdeas.idea: It didn't fit: a 4-hour window at 40 Mbps holds 72 GB, so 90 GB needed two windows and got one
List big releases earlier so they fill over several windows before the unlock
Check each listing against what the window can hold, and alert when a cache won't hold its list in time

coldCase.model: It didn't fit. At 40 Mbps a 4-hour window holds 72 GB, so a 90 GB release needs two windows, and a listing at midnight on Friday gave it only one before the unlock. Going back to 02:00 at full line isn't the answer; that brings back two hours of 900 ms in the final. List big releases earlier, days ahead, so they fill over several windows in quiet hours. And check every listing against what the café's window can hold at its cap before the night: if a cache won't hold its list in time, raise an alert, the way Netflix's operations team monitors appliances that are missing what they should be serving and fixes it before the next fill cycle. Raising the cap for one quiet morning is the last resort, not the plan.
